newsitem.title: USA: Authorities await tests in N.J. prom baby case.
newsitem.headline: Authorities await tests in N.J. prom baby case.

text.p: New Jersey authorities said on Tuesday they were awaiting autopsy results to decide whether to file criminal charges against a teen who gave birth at her high school prom and dumped the newborn in a trash can.
Monmouth County Second Assistant Prosecutor Robert Honecker told Reuters the results of the autopsy on the baby boy would not be available until Wednesday at the earliest.
"The testing is very detailed and the results will be clear cut and irrefutable," he said. "That is why the results may not be ready until tomorrow, or even later in the week."
The mother, identified by fellow students as Melissa Drexler, 18, of Forked River, New Jersey, gave birth at the Lacey Township High School prom dance late on Friday.
She dumped the 6 pound, 6 ounce (2.9 kg) baby in a bathroom trash can and returned to the dance floor, even requesting a song from the disc jockey.

Honecker said the baby's heart was beating in the birth canal, but it was not clear if it breathed outside the mother's body. The infant was born full term, and showed no birth defects or signs of trauma, such as blows.
Microscopic examination of lung tissue will show if the baby breathed after birth and if air in his lungs was produced by breathing on his own or from rescuers who attempted to revive him.
A cleaning woman found the dead baby at the hall where the dance was being held. Drexler has not been arrested.
Students said she was an only child with doting middle-class parents, and planned a career in fashion. No one had known she was pregnant, and she wore a loose-fitting dark dress to the dance.
Officials at Lacey Township High School have told students not to speak to reporters. "Right now we just want to get through today," principal Michael Adamski said.
The incident shocked the middle-class town of Forked River, a tight-knit community of about 22,000 people about 40 miles (64 km) south of New York on New Jersey's Atlantic shore.
"I think she just panicked," Maureen Cable, 15, a student at the high school said. "I think the school should let the students talk about this."
